sweep_summary: Three title-hits for Chimila, all by Terry Malone (SIL). (1) Malone 1997-98 'Mora, minimal foot and segmental phonology in Chimila' (ELC 16:19-70) is not digitized by UCR (site now 404 / old archive lacks it) but Google Books snippets give a verbatim stress rule: primary stress by intensity almost always on the first syllable, secondary stress (phonetic high pitch) on the 3rd and alternating syllables of 4+-syllable words or on non-initial closed syllables, bimoraic trochees left-to-right, bimoraic minimal word, final extrametricality; high priority to acquire in print. (2) Malone 2010 'Nasality and nasal prosody in Chimila' (IJAL 76:1-41) is paywalled and about nasal spreading, not word stress; low priority. (3) Malone 1998 'Pitch accent and stress in Chimila' is an unpublished SSILA winter-meeting paper (the author's own bibliography titles it 'pitch accent in Chimila'); no copy found, but its conclusion is summarized by the author. this search of works with stress in the title's main gain: the Notes on Linguistics 2000 volume (ERIC ED456664, open, downloaded and read) contains two first-hand Malone articles — 'Is CECIL worth the bother?' (3.1:9-30) states on pp.17-18 that primary stress is almost always on the first syllable, cued by intensity and separate from the pitch accent nucleus, with a restricted underlying tone system obscured by intonational and metric systems; 'Interpreting CECIL frames' (3.2:67-99, pp.90-91) shows MHL trisyllables with primary stress on syllable 1 and pitch accent nucleus on syllable 2. This refines the catalog's 'tonal' coding (based only on the Malone 2006 abstract) to initial primary stress plus privative lexical tone; the catalog's stress-placement field can now be filled from a read text. all finds came from direct downloads (ERIC, archive.org, Google Books feed, Crossref, S2). Everything with.

new_statements.quote: her question confirmed what I had begun to suspect: high pitch was not the main indicator of primary stress, and primary stress was almost always on the first syllable. Although the highest pitch in the phonological word usually was on the leftmost syllable, there were numerous exceptions. In addition, high pitch sometimes was behaving as if it belonged to a phonological subsystem separate from intonational pitch. ... Thus the only reliable acoustic correlate of word-level stress for these words was intensity. ... I concluded (Malone 1998a) that Chimila has an underlying restricted tone system which is mostly obscured on the surface by the intonational and metric systems.

new_statements.reading: First-hand, full-text statement by the language's principal analyst: Chimila has fixed (almost always) word-initial primary stress, cued by intensity, running alongside a restricted privative lexical tone system and a phrase-level pitch accent (intonational) system whose high-pitch nucleus usually but not always coincides with the initial stressed syllable (one H per lexical word). The search-snippet evidence Malone 1997-98 (ELC 16) passage adds secondary stress on the 3rd and alternating syllables of 4+-syllable words and left-to-right bimoraic trochees with final extrametricality. So the catalog's 'tonal' coding is incomplete rather than wrong: Chimila is a stress-plus-restricted-tone language with initial primary stress (weight-insensitive at the primary level; quantity/closed syllables matter for secondary stress and footing).

new_statements.quote: The phonology of Chimila still retains several unsolved questions. According to Trillos Amaya (1997: 66), its five vowels (a, e, i, o, u) can be short, long, interrupted (glottalised) and aspirated. Monosyllabic words ending in a long vowel can bear contrastive tone, e.g. to: 'maraca (a musical instrument)' with rising tone, versus to: 'heart' with descending tone. Polysyllabic words contain a tone-bearing syllable of which the tone appears to be partly determined by the nature of a following consonant (descending tone before geminates and r, rising tone before non-geminate obstruents). [...] The interaction between gemination, vowel length, accent and tone in Chimila is a field that requires further investigation. Some of these aspects are discussed in Malone (1997-8).

readall_conflicts: No substantive disagreement. Adelaar & Muysken 2004 (a secondary survey whose Chimila section is based on Trillos Amaya 1997) describe contrastive tone and explicitly leave 'accent' as an open question, referring to Malone (1997-8); Malone's first-hand work already in the catalog (Malone 2000, NOL 3(1): 17-18; Malone 1997-98 ELC 16 snippets; Malone 2001 SWJL 20 snippets) states primary stress almost always on the first syllable, cued by intensity, with a restricted privative H tone and pitch accent phrasing. The survey's deferral is not a contradiction. One caution: the 2004 book's phrasing ('rising' vs 'descending' tone on monosyllables, tone partly determined by the following consonant) follows Trillos Amaya's analysis rather than Malone's, so the two describe the tonal side in different frameworks. The word-final-stress fragment the search returned is about Cholón, not Chimila.

audit.recode_to: Stress + lexical tone, not tonal-only: primary word stress fixed INITIAL ('Primary word stress is predictable, occurring on the first syllable of the word, except in a handful of partially assimilated loans from Spanish that retain stress patterns of the source language' -- Malone 2001, SWJL 20(1) body; 'leftmost syllable of lexemes.. This is also the syllable that bears primary stress at the level of the prosodic word'), metrical structure = bimoraic trochees built left-to-right with pitch fixing secondary accent (Malone 1997-98 'Chimila constructs bimoraic trochaic feet'; 'pitch does, however, determine the locus of secondary accent'; Campbell & Grondona 2012 summarising Malone 2006: 'primary and secondary stresses parsed in bimoraic trochees from left to right, with extrametricality of the..'), combined with a privative/culminative lexical H tone (H vs zero; 'only the leftmost two syllables of roots are marked for tone' Malone 2001; one surface H per phonological word, Malone 2006:42 via Hyman 2010:381). Catalog fields: kind fixed (initial) + tone note 'lexical privative H, culminative', rule 'initial', domain word, exceptions = unassimilated Spanish loans, grade snippet (upgrade to publisher-text once Malone 2001 pp.71-117 or Malone 2006 pp.30-52 are read).

sources.note: Title/record only: a 9-page study of Chimila vowel length by the grammar's author. Trillos Amaya's analysis (as reported by Adelaar & Muysken 2004:75) locates the contrastive rising vs. falling tone on long vowels of monosyllables and ties polysyllabic tone shape to following geminates, so a paper on vowel length very likely discusses the tone-length interaction; content not seen.
